Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Economy Government’s key test in managing debt lies in 2027 – KPMG UNDP report Source : Joy Business 22 November 2026 11:59pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The KPMG UNDP 2027 Budget Highlights says the government's key test in managing Ghana’s public debt lies in 2027, when about GH¢53 billion of Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP) obligations and US$1.17 billion of Eurobond payments fall due.
The Cedi Sinking Fund held GH¢29 billion as at 11 November 2026, enough to cover the February 2027 principal (now offered for early redemption), while the US Dollar Sinking Fund is projected to reach about US$600 million by December 2026.
According to the highlights, sustaining monthly Sinking Fund transfers (7% of non-oil tax revenue), lengthening the domestic maturity profile and keeping debt near the 45% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) anchor will be critical as the deficit widens to 2.9% of GDP in 2027.
Ghana’s 2027 Budget shows that the country’s debt position remains stable, although the KPMG/UNDP report warned that significant repayment obligations for 2027 will test the durability of the debt management framework, anchored on the fiscal consolidation achieved in 2025 and sustained through 2026.
As of end-October 2026, provisional total public debt stood at GH¢759.3 billion (US$65.3 billion), up from GH¢641.1 billion (US$61.3 billion) at end-2025.
“Although the debt-to-GDP ratio rose to 47.5% from 44.7% at the end of 2025, it remains well below the 61.6% recorded at the end of 2024 and the ECOWAS convergence ceiling of 70%. The 18.4% increase in the debt stock was driven mainly by domestic debt, which rose by 28.2% to GH¢427.9 billion, while external debt increased by 7.8% to GH¢331.4 billion. Domestic debt now accounts for 56.4% of total public debt (external: 43.6%), consistent with the government’s strategy to reduce external exposure and limit exchange rate valuation effects”, the report said.
Similarly, lower Treasury bill rates kept interest payments in October 2026 at GH¢38.8 billion, 24.7% below target, it mentioned
The 2026 Debt Sustainability Analysis rates Ghana’s risk of external and overall debt distress as moderate, supporting rating upgrades by Fitch (‘B’) and Moody’s (‘B3’) in 2026.
The report added that the government has remained current on its restructured obligations, paying GH¢10.8 billion to DDEP bondholders in August 2026 (GH¢41.36 billion since 2025) and US$700 million to Eurobond holders in July 2026 (US$2.1 billion since 2025).
Bilateral restructuring agreements have been signed with 16 of 24 official creditor countries, with four more expected by the end of December 2026, alongside four commercial debt agreements.
